In describing the day as great, together with the standing of people before Allah in humility, and describing Him, glorified is He, as Lord of the worlds, there is an indication of the gravity of the sin of defrauding, its great wrong, and the horror of its punishment.

It is said that the intended meaning of His saying "the day when mankind stands" is their standing in their sweat up to the middle of their ears. It is said that the intended meaning is their standing to account for the rights of the servants. It is said that the intended meaning is the standing of the messengers before Allah for judgment. The first view is the preferred one.

His saying "kalla" is for restraint and rebuke of the defrauders who are heedless of the resurrection and what follows it.

Then He resumed, saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. According to Abu Hatim, "kalla" here means "truly," connected to what follows, in the sense: truly, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.

Sijjin is what He explained by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is? It is a written record﴾. So He informed by this that it is a written record, i.e., inscribed. It is said that it is a register comprising the deeds of evil issuing from the devils, the disbelievers and the wrongdoers, and the word "Sijjin" is its proper name.

Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and Ka'b said: It is a rock beneath the seventh earth which is overturned, so that the record of the wicked is placed beneath it. Mujahid also said this. In that case, according to this view, there is an omitted genitive in the sentence, and the implied meaning is: the place of a written record.

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: "la-fi Sijjin" means "in confinement and severe narrowness," and the meaning is: as if they were in a prison, which is taken as a sign of the baseness of their rank and its humiliation.

Al-Wahidi said: Some people said that His saying "a written record" is an explanation of "Sijjin," but this is far-fetched, because Sijjin is not part of the record in anything, according to what we have related from the exegetes. The proper view is that it be taken as an explanation of "record" mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked﴾, on the supposition "it is a written record," i.e., inscribed, whose letters have been made clear. End of quotation. The preferred view is what we have mentioned, and the meaning is: indeed, the record of the wicked, among whom are the defrauders, i.e., what is written of their deeds or the writing of their deeds, is in that register that records vices and is specific to evil, and it is Sijjin.

Then He mentioned what indicates its terror and greatness, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ Then He explained it by His saying: "It is a written record."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of His saying "And what will make you know what Sijjin is?" is that this is not something you or your people knew.

Qatadah said: The meaning of "marqum" (inscribed) is: it has been inscribed for them with evil, as if they were marked with a sign by which it is known that he is a disbeliever.

Muqatil said the same.

They differed regarding the nun of "Sijjin." It is said that it is original, and its derivation is from "sijn," which means confinement, and it is an intensive pattern like khimmir, sikkir and fisseeq, from khamr (wine), sukr (intoxication) and fisq (wickedness).

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj also said this.

Al-Wahidi said: This is weak, because the Arabs did not know "Sijjin."

It is answered that the transmission of these imams is authoritative and indicates that it is from the language of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"A company striking the white swords in the bright forenoon, a striking that the heroes bequeathed, Sijjina."

It is also said that the nun is a substitute for the lam, and the original is "sijjil," derived from "sijil," which is the book.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Whoever says that Sijjin is a place, then "kitab" (record) is nominative as the predicate of "inna," and the adverbial phrase "la-fi Sijjin" is then discarded; and whoever makes it an expression for the record, then "kitab" is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is a record, and this statement explains what Sijjin is. Thus he said.

Al-Dahhak said: "Marqum" means sealed, in the language of Himyar, and the root of "raqm" is writing.

The poet said:

"I shall inscribe to you with clear water, despite your distance, if water has an inscriber."

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾. This is connected to His saying: ﴿the day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. The meaning is: woe on the Day of Resurrection to whoever has denied the resurrection and what the messengers brought.

Then He, glorified is He, identified these deniers, saying: ﴿Who deny the Day of Judgment﴾. The relative clause is an attribute of "the deniers," or a substitute for it.

﴿And none deny it except every transgressor, sinful﴾, i.e., every wicked, oppressive one who exceeds bounds in sin and is absorbed in its causes.

﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, those revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿he says: "Legends of the ancients."﴾ (p-1597) i.e., their tales and falsehoods which they embellished.

Al-Jumhur read "idha tutla" with two taws (the verb with a feminine form). Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and al-Sulami read it with a yā' (masculine form).

His saying "kalla" is for restraint and rebuke of the transgressor, the sinner, from that false statement, and a denial of it. His saying: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾ explains the cause that led them to say that the Qur'an is legends of the ancients.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "raana 'ala qulubihim" means it overcame them with rayn and ruyun (covering). Whatever overcomes and prevails over you has "raana" you and "raana 'alayka."

Al-Farra' said: It is that sins and transgressions multiplied among them until they enveloped their hearts, and that rust is upon them.

Al-Hasan said: It is sin upon sin until the heart becomes blind.

Mujahid said: The heart is like the palm; he raised his palm: when he sins, it contracts and he closes a finger; when he commits another sin, it contracts and he closes another, until he closes all its fingers, until the heart is sealed. He said: They used to consider that this is the rayn. Then he recited this verse.

Abu Zayd said: One says "qad rīna bil-rajul raynan" when he falls into something from which he cannot escape and has no power against it.

Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: al-rayn (the darkening of the heart by sins) is when the heart is blackened by sins. The taba' (the sealing of the heart) is when it is stamped upon, and it is stronger than al-rayn. The iqfal (the locking of the heart) is stronger than the taba'.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-rayn is like rust that covers the heart, like a thin cloud. Al-ghayn is similar to it.

Then He, glorified is He, repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾. It was also said that ﴿kalla﴾ means "truly," so the meaning is: truly, they, meaning the disbelievers, will never see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Muqatil said: this means that after the reckoning and the account, they will not look at Him in the way the believers look at their Lord.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: just as He veiled them in this world from His oneness, He veils them in the Hereafter from seeing Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: in this verse there is evidence that Allah, mighty and majestic, will be seen on the Day of Resurrection, for otherwise this verse would serve no purpose.

And He, whose praise is exalted, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾. So He informed us that the believers will look, and He informed us that the disbelievers are veiled from Him.

It was also said that this is a figure of speech for their humiliation, by comparison with one who is barred from entering upon kings.

Qatadah and Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: it means that He will not look at them with His mercy and will not purify them.

Mujahid said: "veiled" means veiled from His honour. Ibn Kaysan said the same.

﴿Then indeed they will be the ones who burn in the Hellfire﴾: that is, they will enter the Fire and remain in it, not coming out of it. The word thumma (then) indicates the distance in rank, because being burned in Hellfire is more severe than humiliation and being deprived of honour.

﴿Then it will be said: This is what you used to deny﴾: that is, the keepers of Hell will say to them as rebuke and reproach: "This is what you used to deny in the world, so look at it and taste it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No people break a covenant except that Allah gives their enemy power over them, and no people give short measure except that they are deprived of plants and struck with years of drought."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, regarding ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, that a person will be submerged in his sweat up to the middle of his ears.

Al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about this verse, ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾: "How then will it be when Allah gathers you as arrows are gathered in a quiver, for fifty thousand years, and He does not look at you?"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾: "It will be the length of half a day of fifty thousand years. For the believer it will be made easy, like the sun's descent until it sets."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When people are gathered, they will stand for forty years.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from his hadith, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, how long will people stand before the Lord of the worlds on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "A thousand years, during which they are not given permission."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through the chain of Shimr ibn Atiyyah that Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b al-Ahbar about His words: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. He said: The soul of the wicked is raised up to the heaven, but the heaven refuses to accept it. It is then sent down to the earth, but the earth refuses to accept it. It is then taken beneath the seven earths until it reaches Sijjin, which is the cheek of Iblis. A record is brought out for it from beneath the cheek of Iblis, sealed, and placed beneath the cheek of Iblis.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Sijjin is the lowest of the earths.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Al-Falaq is a pit in Hell that is covered, while Sijjin is open." Ibn Kathir said: this is a strange, rejected hadith that is not authentic.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Sijjin is the seventh, lowest earth."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report from Jabir, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abdullah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: When death came to Ka'b, Umm Bishr bint al-Bara' came to him and said: "If you meet my son, convey my greetings to him." He said: "May Allah forgive you, Umm Bishr, we are too preoccupied for that." She said: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The soul of the believer roams in Paradise wherever it wishes, and the soul of the disbeliever is in Sijjin'?" He said: "Yes." She said: "That is it."

Ibn al-Mubarak narrated a similar report from Salman.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When a servant commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart. If he repents, gives it up and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished. If he returns to sin, the spot increases until it covers his heart. That is the rayn which Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in the Qur'an: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered their hearts﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 83, verse 1–17 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Muqatil, and Medinan according to al-Hasan and Ikrimah.

Muqatil also said: It is the first surah to be revealed in Medina.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: It is Medinan except for eight verses, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ to the end of them.

Al-Kalbi and Jabir ibn Zayd said: It was revealed between Mecca and Medina.

Al-Nahhas and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The surah of al-Mutaffifin was revealed in Mecca.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn al-Durays transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The last thing revealed in Mecca was the surah of al-Mutaffifin.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were among the worst of people in measuring, so Allah revealed: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾, and they then measured well thereafter." (al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ — "woe" (waylun) is the subject (mubtada'), and what permitted beginning with an indefinite noun is that it is a supplication. Were it put in the accusative, it would be permissible.

Makki said: The preferred view regarding "woe" and similar words when they are not in construct form is the nominative, though the accusative is permissible; if it is in construct form or definite, the preferred reading is the accusative, such as His saying: ﴿Woe to you, do not invent lies﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. And "to the defrauders" (lil-mutaffifin) is its predicate (khabar).

Al-mutaffif is one who diminishes; its essential meaning is taking a small, slight amount in measuring or weighing, i.e., a meagre, trifling portion.

The lexicographers said: al-mutaffif is derived from al-taffaf, which means little, so the mutaffif is one who diminishes the right of his counterpart by shortchanging him from what is due in measure or weight.

Al-Zajjaj said: The one who shortchanges the measure and the scale is called mutaffif only because he hardly steals anything in measure and weight except a small, trifling amount.

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Mubarrad said: The mutaffif is the one who cheats in measuring and weighing.

The meaning of "woe" (al-waylu) here is intense punishment, or punishment itself, or grave evil, or it is a valley in Hell.

Al-Kalbi said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were giving short measure and weight to others, while taking full measure for themselves, so this verse was revealed."

Al-Suddi said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, there was a man there called Abu Juhayna, who had two saa' measures: he measured with one and took with the other."

Then Allah revealed this verse.

Al-Farra' said: After the revelation of this verse, they became the best of people in measuring until this day of theirs.

Then He, glorified is He, explained who the defrauders are, saying: ﴿Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾, i.e., they take full measure when receiving by measure.

Al-Farra' said: He means "took from people" (ktalu min al-nas), and "ʿala" and "min" in this context are interchangeable; one says iktaltu minka, meaning I took full from you, and iktaltu ʿalayka, meaning I took what was due from you.

Al-Zajjaj said: When they take from people, they demand full measure from them.

He did not mention "ittazanu" (weighing) because measuring and weighing are both used in buying and selling, so one of them indicates the other.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: he means those who, when they buy for themselves, take full measure and weight, and when they sell and weigh for others, they cut short.

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And when they measure for them or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾, i.e., they measure for them or weigh for them; the preposition "lam" is omitted, so the verb reaches its object directly. It is of the type of ḥadhf wa-īṣāl (omission and direct attachment), similar to "naṣahtuka" and "naṣahtu laka" (I advised you). Thus said al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: I heard a Bedouin woman say: "When the people return, we come to the merchant and he measures for us a mudd or two mudds until the coming season."

He said: This is from the speech of the people of Hijaz and those neighbouring them from Qays.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is not permissible to pause on "kalu" until it is joined to the pronoun. Some people make it an emphasis (tawkid), namely an emphasis for the concealed pronoun in the verb, and so they permit pausing on "kalu" or "wazanu."

Abu 'Ubayd said: (p-1596) ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar used to treat them as two separate words and would pause on "kalu" or "wazanu," then say: "hum yukhsirun" (they cause loss).

He said: I think Hamza's reading is like that.

Abu 'Ubayd said: The preferred view is that they are one word, for two reasons: first, the script, which is why they wrote them without an alif; had they been separate, they would have been written "kalu" or "wazanu" with an alif. The second is that one says kiltuka and wazantuka, meaning kiltu laka and wazantu laka, and this is good Arabic, as one says sadaqtuka and sadaqtu laka, and kasabtuka and kasabtu laka, and shakartuka and shakartu laka, and the like.

It is also said that it is by omitting the first term and placing the second term in its position, the omitted term being "the measured thing" and "the weighed thing": i.e., when they measure their measure, or weigh their weight. The meaning of "yukhsirun" is "they diminish," as in His saying: ﴿And do not diminish the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 9]. The Arabs say: khasiratu al-mizan and akhsartuhu (I caused the balance to lose).

Then He, glorified is He, warned them, saying: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ The sentence is resumptive, brought to magnify what they did of defrauding and to make it appalling, and to express wonder at their state in daring to do it. The reference in "ulā'ika" is to the defrauders. The meaning is that they do not entertain the thought that they will be resurrected and then be questioned about what they do.

It is said that "al-zann" (thinking) here means certainty: i.e., those people do not have certainty; had they been certain, they would not have diminished measure and weight. It is also said that "al-zann" retains its usual meaning, and the meaning is: if they do not hold certain belief in the resurrection, why did they not at least suppose it, so that they would reflect on it, investigate it, and abandon what they fear the consequences of?

The great day is the Day of Resurrection; it is described as great because it is a time for those great events of resurrection, reckoning and punishment, and the entry of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire.

Then He informed about that day, saying: ﴿The day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾. The accusative of the time-expression depends on "mab'uthun" mentioned before it, or on a verb implied by "mab'uthun."

That is: they will be raised on the day when mankind stands. Or it is in apposition to the position of "li-yawmin," or by implying "a'nī" (I mean), or it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the genitive position as an apposition to the word "li-yawmin." It is built on the fatha in these two cases because it is attached to a verb.

Then He, glorified is He, repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾. It was also said that ﴿kalla﴾ means "truly," so the meaning is: truly, they, meaning the disbelievers, will never see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Muqatil said: this means that after the reckoning and the account, they will not look at Him in the way the believers look at their Lord.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: just as He veiled them in this world from His oneness, He veils them in the Hereafter from seeing Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: in this verse there is evidence that Allah, mighty and majestic, will be seen on the Day of Resurrection, for otherwise this verse would serve no purpose.

And He, whose praise is exalted, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾. So He informed us that the believers will look, and He informed us that the disbelievers are veiled from Him.

It was also said that this is a figure of speech for their humiliation, by comparison with one who is barred from entering upon kings.

Qatadah and Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: it means that He will not look at them with His mercy and will not purify them.

Mujahid said: "veiled" means veiled from His honour. Ibn Kaysan said the same.

﴿Then indeed they will be the ones who burn in the Hellfire﴾: that is, they will enter the Fire and remain in it, not coming out of it. The word thumma (then) indicates the distance in rank, because being burned in Hellfire is more severe than humiliation and being deprived of honour.

﴿Then it will be said: This is what you used to deny﴾: that is, the keepers of Hell will say to them as rebuke and reproach: "This is what you used to deny in the world, so look at it and taste it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No people break a covenant except that Allah gives their enemy power over them, and no people give short measure except that they are deprived of plants and struck with years of drought."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, regarding ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, that a person will be submerged in his sweat up to the middle of his ears.

Al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about this verse, ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾: "How then will it be when Allah gathers you as arrows are gathered in a quiver, for fifty thousand years, and He does not look at you?"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾: "It will be the length of half a day of fifty thousand years. For the believer it will be made easy, like the sun's descent until it sets."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When people are gathered, they will stand for forty years.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from his hadith, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, how long will people stand before the Lord of the worlds on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "A thousand years, during which they are not given permission."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through the chain of Shimr ibn Atiyyah that Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b al-Ahbar about His words: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. He said: The soul of the wicked is raised up to the heaven, but the heaven refuses to accept it. It is then sent down to the earth, but the earth refuses to accept it. It is then taken beneath the seven earths until it reaches Sijjin, which is the cheek of Iblis. A record is brought out for it from beneath the cheek of Iblis, sealed, and placed beneath the cheek of Iblis.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Sijjin is the lowest of the earths.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Al-Falaq is a pit in Hell that is covered, while Sijjin is open." Ibn Kathir said: this is a strange, rejected hadith that is not authentic.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Sijjin is the seventh, lowest earth."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report from Jabir, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abdullah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: When death came to Ka'b, Umm Bishr bint al-Bara' came to him and said: "If you meet my son, convey my greetings to him." He said: "May Allah forgive you, Umm Bishr, we are too preoccupied for that." She said: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The soul of the believer roams in Paradise wherever it wishes, and the soul of the disbeliever is in Sijjin'?" He said: "Yes." She said: "That is it."

Ibn al-Mubarak narrated a similar report from Salman.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When a servant commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart. If he repents, gives it up and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished. If he returns to sin, the spot increases until it covers his heart. That is the rayn which Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in the Qur'an: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered their hearts﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 83, verse 1–17 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Muqatil, and Medinan according to al-Hasan and Ikrimah.

Muqatil also said: It is the first surah to be revealed in Medina.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: It is Medinan except for eight verses, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ to the end of them.

Al-Kalbi and Jabir ibn Zayd said: It was revealed between Mecca and Medina.

Al-Nahhas and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The surah of al-Mutaffifin was revealed in Mecca.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn al-Durays transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The last thing revealed in Mecca was the surah of al-Mutaffifin.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were among the worst of people in measuring, so Allah revealed: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾, and they then measured well thereafter." (al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ — "woe" (waylun) is the subject (mubtada'), and what permitted beginning with an indefinite noun is that it is a supplication. Were it put in the accusative, it would be permissible.

Makki said: The preferred view regarding "woe" and similar words when they are not in construct form is the nominative, though the accusative is permissible; if it is in construct form or definite, the preferred reading is the accusative, such as His saying: ﴿Woe to you, do not invent lies﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. And "to the defrauders" (lil-mutaffifin) is its predicate (khabar).

Al-mutaffif is one who diminishes; its essential meaning is taking a small, slight amount in measuring or weighing, i.e., a meagre, trifling portion.

The lexicographers said: al-mutaffif is derived from al-taffaf, which means little, so the mutaffif is one who diminishes the right of his counterpart by shortchanging him from what is due in measure or weight.

Al-Zajjaj said: The one who shortchanges the measure and the scale is called mutaffif only because he hardly steals anything in measure and weight except a small, trifling amount.

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Mubarrad said: The mutaffif is the one who cheats in measuring and weighing.

The meaning of "woe" (al-waylu) here is intense punishment, or punishment itself, or grave evil, or it is a valley in Hell.

Al-Kalbi said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were giving short measure and weight to others, while taking full measure for themselves, so this verse was revealed."

Al-Suddi said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, there was a man there called Abu Juhayna, who had two saa' measures: he measured with one and took with the other."

Then Allah revealed this verse.

Al-Farra' said: After the revelation of this verse, they became the best of people in measuring until this day of theirs.

Then He, glorified is He, explained who the defrauders are, saying: ﴿Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾, i.e., they take full measure when receiving by measure.

Al-Farra' said: He means "took from people" (ktalu min al-nas), and "ʿala" and "min" in this context are interchangeable; one says iktaltu minka, meaning I took full from you, and iktaltu ʿalayka, meaning I took what was due from you.

Al-Zajjaj said: When they take from people, they demand full measure from them.

He did not mention "ittazanu" (weighing) because measuring and weighing are both used in buying and selling, so one of them indicates the other.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: he means those who, when they buy for themselves, take full measure and weight, and when they sell and weigh for others, they cut short.

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And when they measure for them or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾, i.e., they measure for them or weigh for them; the preposition "lam" is omitted, so the verb reaches its object directly. It is of the type of ḥadhf wa-īṣāl (omission and direct attachment), similar to "naṣahtuka" and "naṣahtu laka" (I advised you). Thus said al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: I heard a Bedouin woman say: "When the people return, we come to the merchant and he measures for us a mudd or two mudds until the coming season."

He said: This is from the speech of the people of Hijaz and those neighbouring them from Qays.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is not permissible to pause on "kalu" until it is joined to the pronoun. Some people make it an emphasis (tawkid), namely an emphasis for the concealed pronoun in the verb, and so they permit pausing on "kalu" or "wazanu."

Abu 'Ubayd said: (p-1596) ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar used to treat them as two separate words and would pause on "kalu" or "wazanu," then say: "hum yukhsirun" (they cause loss).

He said: I think Hamza's reading is like that.

Abu 'Ubayd said: The preferred view is that they are one word, for two reasons: first, the script, which is why they wrote them without an alif; had they been separate, they would have been written "kalu" or "wazanu" with an alif. The second is that one says kiltuka and wazantuka, meaning kiltu laka and wazantu laka, and this is good Arabic, as one says sadaqtuka and sadaqtu laka, and kasabtuka and kasabtu laka, and shakartuka and shakartu laka, and the like.

It is also said that it is by omitting the first term and placing the second term in its position, the omitted term being "the measured thing" and "the weighed thing": i.e., when they measure their measure, or weigh their weight. The meaning of "yukhsirun" is "they diminish," as in His saying: ﴿And do not diminish the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 9]. The Arabs say: khasiratu al-mizan and akhsartuhu (I caused the balance to lose).

Then He, glorified is He, warned them, saying: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ The sentence is resumptive, brought to magnify what they did of defrauding and to make it appalling, and to express wonder at their state in daring to do it. The reference in "ulā'ika" is to the defrauders. The meaning is that they do not entertain the thought that they will be resurrected and then be questioned about what they do.

It is said that "al-zann" (thinking) here means certainty: i.e., those people do not have certainty; had they been certain, they would not have diminished measure and weight. It is also said that "al-zann" retains its usual meaning, and the meaning is: if they do not hold certain belief in the resurrection, why did they not at least suppose it, so that they would reflect on it, investigate it, and abandon what they fear the consequences of?

The great day is the Day of Resurrection; it is described as great because it is a time for those great events of resurrection, reckoning and punishment, and the entry of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire.

Then He informed about that day, saying: ﴿The day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾. The accusative of the time-expression depends on "mab'uthun" mentioned before it, or on a verb implied by "mab'uthun."

That is: they will be raised on the day when mankind stands. Or it is in apposition to the position of "li-yawmin," or by implying "a'nī" (I mean), or it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the genitive position as an apposition to the word "li-yawmin." It is built on the fatha in these two cases because it is attached to a verb.

Al-Zajjaj said: "yawma" is in the accusative by His saying "mab'uthun," the meaning being: do they not think that they will be raised on the Day of Resurrection? The meaning of "yawma yaqumu al-nas" is: the day when they rise from their graves for the command of the Lord of the worlds, or for His recompense, or for His reckoning, or for His judgment and decree.

In describing the day as great, together with the standing of people before Allah in humility, and describing Him, glorified is He, as Lord of the worlds, there is an indication of the gravity of the sin of defrauding, its great wrong, and the horror of its punishment.

It is said that the intended meaning of His saying "the day when mankind stands" is their standing in their sweat up to the middle of their ears. It is said that the intended meaning is their standing to account for the rights of the servants. It is said that the intended meaning is the standing of the messengers before Allah for judgment. The first view is the preferred one.

His saying "kalla" is for restraint and rebuke of the defrauders who are heedless of the resurrection and what follows it.

Then He resumed, saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. According to Abu Hatim, "kalla" here means "truly," connected to what follows, in the sense: truly, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.

Sijjin is what He explained by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is? It is a written record﴾. So He informed by this that it is a written record, i.e., inscribed. It is said that it is a register comprising the deeds of evil issuing from the devils, the disbelievers and the wrongdoers, and the word "Sijjin" is its proper name.

Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and Ka'b said: It is a rock beneath the seventh earth which is overturned, so that the record of the wicked is placed beneath it. Mujahid also said this. In that case, according to this view, there is an omitted genitive in the sentence, and the implied meaning is: the place of a written record.

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: "la-fi Sijjin" means "in confinement and severe narrowness," and the meaning is: as if they were in a prison, which is taken as a sign of the baseness of their rank and its humiliation.

Al-Wahidi said: Some people said that His saying "a written record" is an explanation of "Sijjin," but this is far-fetched, because Sijjin is not part of the record in anything, according to what we have related from the exegetes. The proper view is that it be taken as an explanation of "record" mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked﴾, on the supposition "it is a written record," i.e., inscribed, whose letters have been made clear. End of quotation. The preferred view is what we have mentioned, and the meaning is: indeed, the record of the wicked, among whom are the defrauders, i.e., what is written of their deeds or the writing of their deeds, is in that register that records vices and is specific to evil, and it is Sijjin.

Then He mentioned what indicates its terror and greatness, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ Then He explained it by His saying: "It is a written record."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of His saying "And what will make you know what Sijjin is?" is that this is not something you or your people knew.

Qatadah said: The meaning of "marqum" (inscribed) is: it has been inscribed for them with evil, as if they were marked with a sign by which it is known that he is a disbeliever.

Muqatil said the same.

They differed regarding the nun of "Sijjin." It is said that it is original, and its derivation is from "sijn," which means confinement, and it is an intensive pattern like khimmir, sikkir and fisseeq, from khamr (wine), sukr (intoxication) and fisq (wickedness).

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj also said this.

Al-Wahidi said: This is weak, because the Arabs did not know "Sijjin."

It is answered that the transmission of these imams is authoritative and indicates that it is from the language of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"A company striking the white swords in the bright forenoon, a striking that the heroes bequeathed, Sijjina."

It is also said that the nun is a substitute for the lam, and the original is "sijjil," derived from "sijil," which is the book.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Whoever says that Sijjin is a place, then "kitab" (record) is nominative as the predicate of "inna," and the adverbial phrase "la-fi Sijjin" is then discarded; and whoever makes it an expression for the record, then "kitab" is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is a record, and this statement explains what Sijjin is. Thus he said.

Al-Dahhak said: "Marqum" means sealed, in the language of Himyar, and the root of "raqm" is writing.

The poet said:

"I shall inscribe to you with clear water, despite your distance, if water has an inscriber."

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾. This is connected to His saying: ﴿the day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. The meaning is: woe on the Day of Resurrection to whoever has denied the resurrection and what the messengers brought.

Then He, glorified is He, identified these deniers, saying: ﴿Who deny the Day of Judgment﴾. The relative clause is an attribute of "the deniers," or a substitute for it.

﴿And none deny it except every transgressor, sinful﴾, i.e., every wicked, oppressive one who exceeds bounds in sin and is absorbed in its causes.

﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, those revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿he says: "Legends of the ancients."﴾ (p-1597) i.e., their tales and falsehoods which they embellished.

Al-Jumhur read "idha tutla" with two taws (the verb with a feminine form). Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and al-Sulami read it with a yā' (masculine form).

His saying "kalla" is for restraint and rebuke of the transgressor, the sinner, from that false statement, and a denial of it. His saying: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾ explains the cause that led them to say that the Qur'an is legends of the ancients.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "raana 'ala qulubihim" means it overcame them with rayn and ruyun (covering). Whatever overcomes and prevails over you has "raana" you and "raana 'alayka."

Al-Farra' said: It is that sins and transgressions multiplied among them until they enveloped their hearts, and that rust is upon them.

Al-Hasan said: It is sin upon sin until the heart becomes blind.

Mujahid said: The heart is like the palm; he raised his palm: when he sins, it contracts and he closes a finger; when he commits another sin, it contracts and he closes another, until he closes all its fingers, until the heart is sealed. He said: They used to consider that this is the rayn. Then he recited this verse.

Abu Zayd said: One says "qad rīna bil-rajul raynan" when he falls into something from which he cannot escape and has no power against it.

Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: al-rayn (the darkening of the heart by sins) is when the heart is blackened by sins. The taba' (the sealing of the heart) is when it is stamped upon, and it is stronger than al-rayn. The iqfal (the locking of the heart) is stronger than the taba'.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Ibn al-Durays transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The last thing revealed in Mecca was the surah of al-Mutaffifin.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were among the worst of people in measuring, so Allah revealed: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾, and they then measured well thereafter." (al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ — "woe" (waylun) is the subject (mubtada'), and what permitted beginning with an indefinite noun is that it is a supplication. Were it put in the accusative, it would be permissible.

Makki said: The preferred view regarding "woe" and similar words when they are not in construct form is the nominative, though the accusative is permissible; if it is in construct form or definite, the preferred reading is the accusative, such as His saying: ﴿Woe to you, do not invent lies﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. And "to the defrauders" (lil-mutaffifin) is its predicate (khabar).

Al-mutaffif is one who diminishes; its essential meaning is taking a small, slight amount in measuring or weighing, i.e., a meagre, trifling portion.

The lexicographers said: al-mutaffif is derived from al-taffaf, which means little, so the mutaffif is one who diminishes the right of his counterpart by shortchanging him from what is due in measure or weight.

Al-Zajjaj said: The one who shortchanges the measure and the scale is called mutaffif only because he hardly steals anything in measure and weight except a small, trifling amount.

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Mubarrad said: The mutaffif is the one who cheats in measuring and weighing.

The meaning of "woe" (al-waylu) here is intense punishment, or punishment itself, or grave evil, or it is a valley in Hell.

Al-Kalbi said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were giving short measure and weight to others, while taking full measure for themselves, so this verse was revealed."

Al-Suddi said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, there was a man there called Abu Juhayna, who had two saa' measures: he measured with one and took with the other."

Then Allah revealed this verse.

Al-Farra' said: After the revelation of this verse, they became the best of people in measuring until this day of theirs.

Then He, glorified is He, explained who the defrauders are, saying: ﴿Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾, i.e., they take full measure when receiving by measure.

Al-Farra' said: He means "took from people" (ktalu min al-nas), and "ʿala" and "min" in this context are interchangeable; one says iktaltu minka, meaning I took full from you, and iktaltu ʿalayka, meaning I took what was due from you.

Al-Zajjaj said: When they take from people, they demand full measure from them.

He did not mention "ittazanu" (weighing) because measuring and weighing are both used in buying and selling, so one of them indicates the other.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: he means those who, when they buy for themselves, take full measure and weight, and when they sell and weigh for others, they cut short.

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And when they measure for them or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾, i.e., they measure for them or weigh for them; the preposition "lam" is omitted, so the verb reaches its object directly. It is of the type of ḥadhf wa-īṣāl (omission and direct attachment), similar to "naṣahtuka" and "naṣahtu laka" (I advised you). Thus said al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: I heard a Bedouin woman say: "When the people return, we come to the merchant and he measures for us a mudd or two mudds until the coming season."

He said: This is from the speech of the people of Hijaz and those neighbouring them from Qays.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is not permissible to pause on "kalu" until it is joined to the pronoun. Some people make it an emphasis (tawkid), namely an emphasis for the concealed pronoun in the verb, and so they permit pausing on "kalu" or "wazanu."

Abu 'Ubayd said: (p-1596) ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar used to treat them as two separate words and would pause on "kalu" or "wazanu," then say: "hum yukhsirun" (they cause loss).

He said: I think Hamza's reading is like that.

Abu 'Ubayd said: The preferred view is that they are one word, for two reasons: first, the script, which is why they wrote them without an alif; had they been separate, they would have been written "kalu" or "wazanu" with an alif. The second is that one says kiltuka and wazantuka, meaning kiltu laka and wazantu laka, and this is good Arabic, as one says sadaqtuka and sadaqtu laka, and kasabtuka and kasabtu laka, and shakartuka and shakartu laka, and the like.

It is also said that it is by omitting the first term and placing the second term in its position, the omitted term being "the measured thing" and "the weighed thing": i.e., when they measure their measure, or weigh their weight. The meaning of "yukhsirun" is "they diminish," as in His saying: ﴿And do not diminish the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 9]. The Arabs say: khasiratu al-mizan and akhsartuhu (I caused the balance to lose).

Then He, glorified is He, warned them, saying: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ The sentence is resumptive, brought to magnify what they did of defrauding and to make it appalling, and to express wonder at their state in daring to do it. The reference in "ulā'ika" is to the defrauders. The meaning is that they do not entertain the thought that they will be resurrected and then be questioned about what they do.

It is said that "al-zann" (thinking) here means certainty: i.e., those people do not have certainty; had they been certain, they would not have diminished measure and weight. It is also said that "al-zann" retains its usual meaning, and the meaning is: if they do not hold certain belief in the resurrection, why did they not at least suppose it, so that they would reflect on it, investigate it, and abandon what they fear the consequences of?

The great day is the Day of Resurrection; it is described as great because it is a time for those great events of resurrection, reckoning and punishment, and the entry of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire.

Then He informed about that day, saying: ﴿The day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾. The accusative of the time-expression depends on "mab'uthun" mentioned before it, or on a verb implied by "mab'uthun."

That is: they will be raised on the day when mankind stands. Or it is in apposition to the position of "li-yawmin," or by implying "a'nī" (I mean), or it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the genitive position as an apposition to the word "li-yawmin." It is built on the fatha in these two cases because it is attached to a verb.

Al-Zajjaj said: "yawma" is in the accusative by His saying "mab'uthun," the meaning being: do they not think that they will be raised on the Day of Resurrection? The meaning of "yawma yaqumu al-nas" is: the day when they rise from their graves for the command of the Lord of the worlds, or for His recompense, or for His reckoning, or for His judgment and decree.

In describing the day as great, together with the standing of people before Allah in humility, and describing Him, glorified is He, as Lord of the worlds, there is an indication of the gravity of the sin of defrauding, its great wrong, and the horror of its punishment.

It is said that the intended meaning of His saying "the day when mankind stands" is their standing in their sweat up to the middle of their ears. It is said that the intended meaning is their standing to account for the rights of the servants. It is said that the intended meaning is the standing of the messengers before Allah for judgment. The first view is the preferred one.

His saying "kalla" is for restraint and rebuke of the defrauders who are heedless of the resurrection and what follows it.

Then He resumed, saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. According to Abu Hatim, "kalla" here means "truly," connected to what follows, in the sense: truly, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.

Sijjin is what He explained by His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is? It is a written record﴾. So He informed by this that it is a written record, i.e., inscribed. It is said that it is a register comprising the deeds of evil issuing from the devils, the disbelievers and the wrongdoers, and the word "Sijjin" is its proper name.

Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and Ka'b said: It is a rock beneath the seventh earth which is overturned, so that the record of the wicked is placed beneath it. Mujahid also said this. In that case, according to this view, there is an omitted genitive in the sentence, and the implied meaning is: the place of a written record.

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: "la-fi Sijjin" means "in confinement and severe narrowness," and the meaning is: as if they were in a prison, which is taken as a sign of the baseness of their rank and its humiliation.

Al-Wahidi said: Some people said that His saying "a written record" is an explanation of "Sijjin," but this is far-fetched, because Sijjin is not part of the record in anything, according to what we have related from the exegetes. The proper view is that it be taken as an explanation of "record" mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked﴾, on the supposition "it is a written record," i.e., inscribed, whose letters have been made clear. End of quotation. The preferred view is what we have mentioned, and the meaning is: indeed, the record of the wicked, among whom are the defrauders, i.e., what is written of their deeds or the writing of their deeds, is in that register that records vices and is specific to evil, and it is Sijjin.

Then He mentioned what indicates its terror and greatness, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ Then He explained it by His saying: "It is a written record."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of His saying "And what will make you know what Sijjin is?" is that this is not something you or your people knew.

Qatadah said: The meaning of "marqum" (inscribed) is: it has been inscribed for them with evil, as if they were marked with a sign by which it is known that he is a disbeliever.

Muqatil said the same.

They differed regarding the nun of "Sijjin." It is said that it is original, and its derivation is from "sijn," which means confinement, and it is an intensive pattern like khimmir, sikkir and fisseeq, from khamr (wine), sukr (intoxication) and fisq (wickedness).

Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj also said this.

Al-Wahidi said: This is weak, because the Arabs did not know "Sijjin."

It is answered that the transmission of these imams is authoritative and indicates that it is from the language of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"A company striking the white swords in the bright forenoon, a striking that the heroes bequeathed, Sijjina."

It is also said that the nun is a substitute for the lam, and the original is "sijjil," derived from "sijil," which is the book.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Whoever says that Sijjin is a place, then "kitab" (record) is nominative as the predicate of "inna," and the adverbial phrase "la-fi Sijjin" is then discarded; and whoever makes it an expression for the record, then "kitab" is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is a record, and this statement explains what Sijjin is. Thus he said.

Al-Dahhak said: "Marqum" means sealed, in the language of Himyar, and the root of "raqm" is writing.

The poet said:

"I shall inscribe to you with clear water, despite your distance, if water has an inscriber."

﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾. This is connected to His saying: ﴿the day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. The meaning is: woe on the Day of Resurrection to whoever has denied the resurrection and what the messengers brought.

Then He, glorified is He, identified these deniers, saying: ﴿Who deny the Day of Judgment﴾. The relative clause is an attribute of "the deniers," or a substitute for it.

﴿And none deny it except every transgressor, sinful﴾, i.e., every wicked, oppressive one who exceeds bounds in sin and is absorbed in its causes.

﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, those revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿he says: "Legends of the ancients."﴾ (p-1597) i.e., their tales and falsehoods which they embellished.

Al-Jumhur read "idha tutla" with two taws (the verb with a feminine form). Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and al-Sulami read it with a yā' (masculine form).

His saying "kalla" is for restraint and rebuke of the transgressor, the sinner, from that false statement, and a denial of it. His saying: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾ explains the cause that led them to say that the Qur'an is legends of the ancients.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "raana 'ala qulubihim" means it overcame them with rayn and ruyun (covering). Whatever overcomes and prevails over you has "raana" you and "raana 'alayka."

Al-Farra' said: It is that sins and transgressions multiplied among them until they enveloped their hearts, and that rust is upon them.

Al-Hasan said: It is sin upon sin until the heart becomes blind.

Mujahid said: The heart is like the palm; he raised his palm: when he sins, it contracts and he closes a finger; when he commits another sin, it contracts and he closes another, until he closes all its fingers, until the heart is sealed. He said: They used to consider that this is the rayn. Then he recited this verse.

Abu Zayd said: One says "qad rīna bil-rajul raynan" when he falls into something from which he cannot escape and has no power against it.

Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: al-rayn (the darkening of the heart by sins) is when the heart is blackened by sins. The taba' (the sealing of the heart) is when it is stamped upon, and it is stronger than al-rayn. The iqfal (the locking of the heart) is stronger than the taba'.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-rayn is like rust that covers the heart, like a thin cloud. Al-ghayn is similar to it.

Then He, glorified is He, repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿No! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾. It was also said that ﴿kalla﴾ means "truly," so the meaning is: truly, they, meaning the disbelievers, will never see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Muqatil said: this means that after the reckoning and the account, they will not look at Him in the way the believers look at their Lord.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: just as He veiled them in this world from His oneness, He veils them in the Hereafter from seeing Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: in this verse there is evidence that Allah, mighty and majestic, will be seen on the Day of Resurrection, for otherwise this verse would serve no purpose.

And He, whose praise is exalted, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾. So He informed us that the believers will look, and He informed us that the disbelievers are veiled from Him.

It was also said that this is a figure of speech for their humiliation, by comparison with one who is barred from entering upon kings.

Qatadah and Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: it means that He will not look at them with His mercy and will not purify them.

Mujahid said: "veiled" means veiled from His honour. Ibn Kaysan said the same.

﴿Then indeed they will be the ones who burn in the Hellfire﴾: that is, they will enter the Fire and remain in it, not coming out of it. The word thumma (then) indicates the distance in rank, because being burned in Hellfire is more severe than humiliation and being deprived of honour.

﴿Then it will be said: This is what you used to deny﴾: that is, the keepers of Hell will say to them as rebuke and reproach: "This is what you used to deny in the world, so look at it and taste it."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No people break a covenant except that Allah gives their enemy power over them, and no people give short measure except that they are deprived of plants and struck with years of drought."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, regarding ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, that a person will be submerged in his sweat up to the middle of his ears.

Al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about this verse, ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾: "How then will it be when Allah gathers you as arrows are gathered in a quiver, for fifty thousand years, and He does not look at you?"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾: "It will be the length of half a day of fifty thousand years. For the believer it will be made easy, like the sun's descent until it sets."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When people are gathered, they will stand for forty years.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from his hadith, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, how long will people stand before the Lord of the worlds on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "A thousand years, during which they are not given permission."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through the chain of Shimr ibn Atiyyah that Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b al-Ahbar about His words: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. He said: The soul of the wicked is raised up to the heaven, but the heaven refuses to accept it. It is then sent down to the earth, but the earth refuses to accept it. It is then taken beneath the seven earths until it reaches Sijjin, which is the cheek of Iblis. A record is brought out for it from beneath the cheek of Iblis, sealed, and placed beneath the cheek of Iblis.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Sijjin is the lowest of the earths.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Al-Falaq is a pit in Hell that is covered, while Sijjin is open." Ibn Kathir said: this is a strange, rejected hadith that is not authentic.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Sijjin is the seventh, lowest earth."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report from Jabir, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abdullah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: When death came to Ka'b, Umm Bishr bint al-Bara' came to him and said: "If you meet my son, convey my greetings to him." He said: "May Allah forgive you, Umm Bishr, we are too preoccupied for that." She said: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The soul of the believer roams in Paradise wherever it wishes, and the soul of the disbeliever is in Sijjin'?" He said: "Yes." She said: "That is it."

Ibn al-Mubarak narrated a similar report from Salman.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When a servant commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart. If he repents, gives it up and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished. If he returns to sin, the spot increases until it covers his heart. That is the rayn which Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in the Qur'an: ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered their hearts﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 83, verses 18–36 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1598) His saying: "Kalla" (no indeed) is for restraining and deterring from what they were upon. The repetition is for emphasis. The clause "Inna kitaba al-abrari lafi 'Illiyyin" (Indeed, the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin) is resumptive, explaining what the previous statement contained. It is also permissible that kalla means "haqqan" (truly). Al-abrar (the righteous) are those who obey, and their record is the pages of their good deeds.

Al-Farra' said: "Illiyyin" is a height upon a height with no end. The reasoning for this is that it is derived from the plural of 'Alliy, from al-'uluww (highness).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is the elevation of places.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is inflected like a plural (ka-i'rab al-jam'), because it has the form of the plural and has no singular from its own form, like thalathin, 'ishrin and qinnasrin. It was said: it is the name of the register of goodness in which the deeds of the righteous are recorded.

Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes that it is the seventh heaven.

Al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatada said: it means the seventh heaven, in which are the spirits of the believers.

Al-Dahhak said: it is Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary), to which everything from the command of Allah reaches and beyond which it does not pass. It was also said that it is Paradise.

Qatada also said: it is above the seventh heaven, at the right-hand pillar of the Throne. It was said that "Illiyyin" is a description of the angels, for they are in the exalted assembly, as one says "fulan fi Bani fulan" (so-and-so is among the sons of so-and-so), meaning among their company.

"Wa ma adraka ma 'Illiyyun. Kitabun marqum" (And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is? A written record). That is: and what will make you know, O Muhammad, what 'Illiyyun is? This is in the manner of magnifying and glorifying 'Illiyyin. Then He explained it, saying: "Kitabun marqum" (a written record), meaning inscribed. The discussion of this is like the earlier discussion in His saying: "Wa ma adraka ma Sijjin. Kitabun marqum" (And what will make you know what Sijjin is? A written record).

The clause "Yashhaduhu al-muqarrabun" (witnessed by those brought near) is another description of "kitab" (record). The meaning is that the angels attend that inscribed record. It was also said that they bear witness to what is in it on the Day of Resurrection.

Wahb and Ibn Ishaq said: "al-muqarrabun" here means Israfil. When the believer does a deed of righteousness, the angels carry the record upward, and it has a light shining through the heavens like the light of the sun on the earth, until they bring it to Israfil, who seals it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their condition in Paradise after mentioning their record, saying: "Inna al-abrara lafi na'im" (Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss). That is: indeed, the people of obedience are in great luxury, whose extent cannot be measured.

"'Ala al-ara'iki yanzurun" (Upon couches, they observe). Al-ara'ik are the beds that are within canopies. It has already been mentioned that the word "arika" is not applied to a bed unless it is within a canopy (hajala).

Al-Hasan said: "We did not know what al-ara'ik were until a man from Yemen came to us, and he claimed that the arika among them is the canopy (hajala) when there is a bed within it."

The meaning of "yanzurun" is that they look at what Allah has prepared for them of honours. So said 'Ikrima, Mujahid and others.

Muqatil said: they look at the people of the Fire. It was also said: they look at His Face and His majesty.

"Ta'rifu fi wujuhihim nadrata al-na'im" (You will recognise in their faces the radiance of bliss). That is: when you see them, you will know that they are among the people of blessing, because of what you see in their faces of light, beauty, whiteness, delight and brightness. The address is to every beholder who is fit for this. It is said: "anda'a al-nabat" (the plant became radiant) when it blossomed and bloomed.

'Ata' said: that is because Allah increased their beauty and their hues with what no describer can describe.

The majority read "ta'rifu" with a fatha on the first letter (ta') and a kasra on the ra', with "nadrata" in the accusative. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Ya'qub, Shayba, Talha and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ra', in the passive form, with "nadratu" in the nominative as the deputy of the subject.

"Yusqawna min raheeqin makhtum" (They will be given to drink of a sealed wine). Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: al-raheeq of wine is that which has no adulteration and nothing that spoils it, and al-makhtum is that which has a seal (khitam).

Al-Khalil said: al-raheeq is the finest wine. In al-Sihah it is said: al-raheeq is the yellowish colour of wine.

Mujahid said: it is the old, white, pure wine. From this is the saying of Hassan:

"They give to drink to whoever comes to al-Baris, upon them,
From the Barada, which is clapped with clear, smooth raheeq."

Mujahid said: "makhtum" means sealed with clay. It seems he took it to mean sealing with clay, and the meaning would be that it is forbidden from being touched by any hand until its seal is broken for the righteous.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: its khitam is the last of its taste, and this is the meaning of His saying: "khitamuhu misk" (its seal is musk). That is: the last of its taste is the scent of musk. When the drinker lifts his mouth from the last of his drink, he finds its scent like the scent of musk.

It was also said that its vessels, including the cups and pitchers, are sealed with musk instead of clay. This seems to be an illustration of its utmost preciousness and the goodness of its fragrance.

The summary is that "makhtum" and "khitam" are either from khitam (the end) of a thing, which is its last part, or from khatm (sealing) of a thing, which is placing a seal upon it, as things are sealed with clay and the like.

The majority read "khitamuhu" (khitamuhu), while 'Ali, 'Alqama, Shaqiq, al-Dahhak, Tawus and al-Kisa'i read "khatamuhu" with a fatha on the kha' and on the ta' and an alif between them.

'Alqama said: Have you not seen a woman say to the perfumer: "Make its khatam musk," meaning its last part? Al-khatam and al-khitam are close in meaning, except that al-khatam is the noun and al-khitam is the verbal noun. So said al-Farra'. In al-Sihah it is said: al-khitam is the clay with which something is sealed. Ibn Zayd also said so.

al-Farazdaq said:

"They spent the night beside me, thrown down,
And I spent the night loosening the locks of the seal."

"Wa fi dhalika fal-yatanafasi al-mutanafisun" (For this let the competitors compete). That is: let those who desire desire it. The indication of "dhalika" is to the raheeq described with that quality. It was said that "fi" here means "ila" (to): that is, to that let those who race hasten in deeds, as in His saying: "li-mithli hadha fal-ya'mali al-'amilun" (for the like of this let the workers work) [al-Saffat: 61]. The root of tanafus is contention over a thing and striving for it, such that each one loves to have it exclusively for himself and not for his companion. It is said: "nafastu al-shay 'alayhi anfusuhu nafasatan," meaning I was stingy with it and did not love that it should reach him.

al-Baghawi said: its origin is from a precious thing that people's souls covet, so each one wants it for himself, and he is stingy with it toward others, that is, he is miserly with it.

'Ata' said: the meaning is "fal-yastabiqi al-mustabiqun" (let those who race outpace one another).

Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "fal-yatanazi'i al-mutanazi'un" (let those who contend contend).

His saying: "Wa mizajuhu min tasnim" (and its mixture is of tasnim), is conjoined to "khitamuhu misk" as another description of raheeq. That is: the mixture of that raheeq is from tasnim, which is a drink that pours down upon them from above. It is the most noble drink of Paradise. The root meaning of tasnim in the language is elevation. It is a spring of water that flows from a height to a lower place. From it comes "sanam al-ba'ir" (the hump of the camel), because of its height above its body, and from it comes "tasnim al-qubur" (the raised form of graves).

Then He explained that, saying: "'Aynan yashrabu biha al-muqarrabun" (a spring from which those brought near will drink). The accusative of "'aynan" is by way of praise.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). It is permissible for "'aynan" to be a circumstantial clause even though it is a solid noun, not a derived one, because it is qualified by His saying: "yashrabu biha" (they drink from it).

Al-Akhfash said: it is governed by "yusqawna" (they are given to drink): that is, they are given to drink a spring, or from a spring.

Al-Farra' said: it is governed by "tasnim," on the basis that it is a verbal noun derived from sanam (hump), as in His saying: "aw it'amun fi yawmin dhi masghabatin yatiman" (or feeding in a day of hunger an orphan) [al-Balad: 14–15].

The first view is preferable, and al-Mubarrad said so.

It was said that the "ba'" in "biha" is extra: that is, "yashrabuha" (they drink it), or it means "min" (from): that is, "yashrabu minha" (they drink from it).

Ibn Zayd said: We have been told that it is a spring that flows from beneath the Throne. It was said: those brought near drink from it pure, and the cup of the people of the right is mixed with it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the ugly deeds of the polytheists, saying: "Inna al-ladhina ajramu" (Indeed, those who committed crimes), and they are the disbelievers of Quraysh and whoever agreed with them in disbelief, "kanu min al-ladhina amanu yadhhakun" (were laughing at those who believed). That is: in the world they used to mock the believers and scoff at them.

"Wa idha marru bihim" (And when they passed by them). That is: when the believers passed by the disbelievers while they were in their gatherings, "yataghammazun" (winking at one another), from al-ghamz, which is the signalling with the eyelids and eyebrows. That is: some of them would wink at others and signal with their eyes and eyebrows. It was also said that they would reproach them and find fault with them for Islam.

"Wa idha inqalabu" (And when they returned). That is, the disbelievers returned to their families from their gatherings, "inqalabu fakihin" (they returned jesting), that is, pleased with what they were in, delighting in it, taking pleasure in mentioning the believers, slandering them, mocking them and ridiculing them.

Al-inqilab means al-insiraf (turning back).

The majority read "fakihin" (fakihina, with alif), while Hafs, Ibn al-Qa'qa', al-A'raj and al-Sulami read "fakihin" without alif.

Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects, like "tamai'" and "tami'" (greedy), and "hadhir" and "hadhir" (cautious). Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Dukhan: that al-fakih is the one who is arrogant and insolent, and al-fakih is the one who is pampered and luxurious.

"Wa idha ra'awhum" (And when they saw them), that is, when the disbelievers saw the Muslims in any place, "qalu inna ha'ula'i ladallun" (they said: indeed these are astray), in following Muhammad, adhering to what he brought, and abandoning present luxury. It is also permissible that the meaning is: when the Muslims saw the disbelievers, they said this statement. The first is preferable.

The clause "Wa ma ursilu 'alayhim hafizin" (They were not sent as guardians over them) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "qalu" (they said). That is: they said that because they were not sent from Allah as guardians over the Muslims, appointed to watch over their conditions and deeds.

"Fal-yawma alladhina amanu" (So today, those who believed), by "al-yawm" is meant the Last Day, "min al-kuffari yadhhakun" (of the disbelievers they laugh). The meaning is that on that day the believers laugh at the disbelievers when they see them humiliated and defeated, and the punishment has descended upon them, just as the disbelievers laughed at them in the world.

The clause "'ala al-ara'iki yanzurun" (upon couches, they observe) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yadhhakun": that is, they laugh at them while looking at them and at their dreadful condition. The explanation of al-ara'ik has been given shortly before.

al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: when the people of Paradise wish, they look from their dwellings at the enemies of Allah being punished in the Fire, and they laugh at them as they laughed at them in the world.

Abu Salih said: it is said to the people of the Fire: "Come out," and its gates are opened for them. When they see that they have been opened, they approach them wanting to come out, while the believers look at them from upon the couches. When they reach its gates, they are shut in their faces. That is His saying: "Fal-yawma alladhina amanu min al-kuffari yadhhakun" (So today, those who believed laugh at the disbelievers).

"Hal thuwwiba al-kuffaru ma kanu yaf'alun" (Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?). The clause is resumptive, to explain that the requital has indeed fallen upon the disbelievers for what they used to do in the world of laughing at the believers and mocking them. The interrogation is for confirmation. "Thuwwiba" means "uthība" (was rewarded). The meaning is: were the disbelievers recompensed for what they used to do to the believers? It was said that the clause is in the accusative position governed by "yanzurun" (they look). It was also said that it is by the implied saying: that is, some believers say to others: "Have the disbelievers been rewarded?" Reward (thawab) is what returns to the servant in return for his deed, and it is used for both good and evil.

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related through the chain of Shimr ibn 'Atiyya that Ibn 'Abbas asked Ka'b al-Ahbar about His saying: "Inna kitaba al-abrari lafi 'Illiyyin." He said: the soul of the believer, when it is taken, is raised up to the heaven. The gates of heaven are opened for it, and the angels meet it with glad tidings until it reaches the Throne, and the angels ascend. Then a scroll comes out for it from beneath the Throne, and it is inscribed and sealed and placed beneath the Throne, as a recognition of salvation for the reckoning of the Day of Religion.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning "lafi 'Illiyyin" that he said: it is Paradise. And concerning His saying: "Yashhaduhu al-muqarrabun," he said: the people of heaven.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Umama who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A prayer after a prayer with no idle talk between them is a record in 'Illiyyin."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib concerning His saying: "nadrata al-na'im" (the radiance of bliss), that he said: it is a spring in Paradise in which they perform ablution and bathe, so the radiance of bliss flows upon them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Hannad, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: "Yusqawna min raheeqin makhtum," that he said: al-raheeq is wine, and al-makhtum: they find its final outcome to be the taste of musk.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 83, verses 18–36 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him (Ibn Abbas), regarding His words: (sealed) he said: "mixed." (Its seal is musk) he said: "its taste and its scent."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th (The Resurrection) narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "of a pure wine," he said: "wine," and regarding His words: "sealed," he said: "it was sealed with musk."

al-Firyabi, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿Its seal is musk﴾, he said: "It is not a seal with which it is sealed, but its admixture is musk. Have you not seen the woman among your women who says, 'its admixture is such-and-such perfume'?"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Darda', regarding "its seal is musk," he said: "It is a white drink like silver, with which they seal the end of their drink. Were a man of the people of this world to put his fingers into it and then take them out, no living soul would remain without smelling its fragrance."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Tasnim (a spring in Paradise) is the most noble drink of the people of Paradise. It is pure for the muqarrabun (those brought near), and it is mixed for the companions of the right hand" (p-١٦٠٠).

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿And its mixture is of Tasnim﴾, he said: "It is a spring in Paradise, mixed for the companions of the right hand, and the muqarrabun drink it pure."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about His words: ﴿And its mixture is of Tasnim﴾, and he said: "This is of what Allah has spoken of: ﴿No soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17]."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 83, verses 18–36 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1598) His saying: "Kalla" (no indeed) is for restraining and deterring from what they were upon. The repetition is for emphasis.
